learningObjectives: Create an image-based control using Advanced Identification in XScan.
Explain why Image-Based Test Automation is positioned as a last-resort identification method.
Apply the multi-screenshot technique for controls that do not always look the same.
Distinguish image-based identification from anchor-based identification and state the anchor rules.

elements.term: Identifying by what it looks like
elements.description: Every identification method covered so far works on structure — properties, the control tree, the UI Automation interface. Image-based identification abandons structure entirely and identifies a control by one or more screenshots of it. Tosca finds the control by locating that image on screen at execution time.

In XScan, select the control you want to identify, then in the Identification methods pane choose ADVANCED IDENTIFICATION → IMAGE. You then supply the screenshot or screenshots that represent the control.

elements.text: Tricentis' own positioning is explicit: image-based identification is recommended for controls where nothing else works. It is a fallback, not a convenience. Reaching for it early produces automation that breaks on a theme change, a font update, a different screen resolution, or a browser zoom level — none of which would trouble structural identification.

bulletPoints: XScan → select control → ADVANCED IDENTIFICATION → IMAGE.
Documented as the method for controls where nothing else works.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Making image identification as reliable as it can be

elements.description: The single most useful technique in this lesson: supply more than one screenshot to identify a control, especially when the control does not always look the same. A button with hover, focused, and default states, or an icon that changes slightly by context, will fail against a single reference image but match reliably against a set covering its variations.

Multiple screenshots handle variation the control was designed to have. They do not protect against changes to the environment: display scaling, resolution, colour scheme or theme, anti-aliasing differences between machines, or a redesign. This is why image-based controls are also the most machine-sensitive form of automation — a TestCase that passes on the author's laptop can fail on an execution agent with different display settings.

bulletPoints: More than one screenshot = the fix for controls with several visual states.
Screenshots cannot absorb resolution, scaling or theme differences — plan execution environments accordingly.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: The other Advanced Identification method: Anchor

elements.description: Sitting alongside IMAGE in the same pane is ANCHOR — select the control, then ADVANCED IDENTIFICATION → ANCHOR. Rather than matching appearance, this identifies the target control by its location in relation to another element, the anchor control. It is often the better answer when a control has no stable properties of its own but sits next to something that does.

elements.title: Anchor rules — the same three you met in the PDF lesson
items: The anchor control must be a text or an image.
It must be uniquely identifiable — repetitive areas cannot be used as anchors.
It must be on the same page as the target control.

elements.text: This consistency is worth noticing: anchors work the same way whether you are scanning a PDF with the PDF Engine or a UI control in XScan. Learn the three rules once and they apply in both places.

bulletPoints: ANCHOR and IMAGE are siblings under Advanced Identification — try ANCHOR first.
Anchor rules are identical to the PDF Engine's: text or image · unique · same page.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Where this sits in the escalation path

elements.title: Full order of preference
items: 1. Standard identification by properties — the default and the goal.
2. Anchor-based identification — when the control has no stable properties but a stable neighbour.
3. Alternative engine — for Windows, rescanning with UIA instead of WinX or vice versa (Lesson 4).
4. Custom control — a DLL that makes Tosca recognise the widget properly (Lesson 6).
5. Image-based identification — appearance matching, when nothing else works.

elements.text: Self-healing (Lesson 5) does not appear in this list because it is not an identification method — it is a recovery mechanism that operates when the chosen method fails at runtime. It also does not apply to image-based controls, whose supported-engine list does not include an image matcher.
📄 Official Tricentis Academy exercise material for this lesson is not redistributed here — complete the exercises inside the official course.

bulletPoints: Image-based is step 5 of 5 — genuinely the last option, not a shortcut.

examPitfalls.title: Using image-based identification as a first resort
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Switching to IMAGE identification as soon as a control is awkward to identify by properties, because it is quick to set up.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Tricentis recommends image-based identification for controls where nothing else works. Try standard properties, then anchors, then an alternative engine, then a custom control before falling back on appearance matching.

examPitfalls.title: Supplying a single screenshot for a control with several visual states
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Capturing one image of a button and finding the TestCase fails intermittently when the button is hovered or focused.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use more than one screenshot to identify a control, particularly when controls don't always look the same. A set of images covering the variations is what makes image identification usable.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming image-based controls port cleanly between machines
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Authoring image-based controls on a high-DPI laptop and deploying to execution agents with different display settings.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Image matching is sensitive to resolution, display scaling, theme and rendering differences. Screenshots cannot absorb environment changes, so keep the execution environment consistent with where the images were captured.

examPitfalls.title: Confusing anchor identification with image identification
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Treating ANCHOR and IMAGE as the same fallback because they sit next to each other under Advanced Identification.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: ANCHOR identifies a control by its position relative to another element and remains a structural method; IMAGE matches appearance. Anchor is the earlier and more robust option of the two.

examPitfalls.title: Expecting self-healing to rescue an image-based control
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Enabling the SelfHealing TCP and assuming image-identified controls are now resilient too.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Self-healing is supported for DotNet, Java, Oracle, UIA, XBrowser and Salesforce — it works on control properties, which image identification does not use. An image-based control that stops matching has to be recaptured.

practiceQuiz.scenario: According to Tricentis, when should image-based identification be used?

options.text: Whenever it is faster to set up than property-based identification.
For controls where nothing else works — it is a last resort.
For every control in a Windows desktop application.
Only for controls inside PDF documents.

practiceQuiz.hint: The documentation is explicit about its position among the methods.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Image-based identification is recommended for controls where nothing else works. Because it matches appearance rather than structure, it breaks on theme, resolution and rendering changes that structural identification would survive.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A button changes appearance between its default, hovered and focused states, and the image-based control matches only sometimes. What is the recommended fix?

options.text: Lower the match accuracy until all states pass.
Supply more than one screenshot, covering the control's different appearances.
Switch the Module to a different engine.
Take the screenshot at a higher resolution.

practiceQuiz.hint: The documented technique addresses controls that don't always look the same.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Tricentis recommends using more than one screenshot to identify a control, especially when controls don't always look the same. A set of reference images covering each visual state makes the identification reliable.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Where in XScan do you configure image-based identification for a control?

options.text: In the Module's Self-Healing Properties tab.
In the Identification methods pane: ADVANCED IDENTIFICATION → IMAGE.
In Project Settings → Engines.
By right-clicking the application tile during the scan.

practiceQuiz.hint: It lives next to the ANCHOR option.
practiceQuiz.rationale: You select the control and then choose ADVANCED IDENTIFICATION → IMAGE in the Identification methods pane. ANCHOR is the sibling option in the same pane.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which conditions must an anchor control satisfy when using anchor-based identification? (three correct answers)

options.text: It must be a text or an image.
It must be uniquely identifiable — repetitive areas cannot be used.
It must be on the same page as the target control.
It must have been captured as a screenshot first.

practiceQuiz.hint: The same three rules apply here as in the PDF Engine lesson.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Anchor rules are consistent across Tosca: the anchor must be a text or image, uniquely identifiable (no repetitive areas), and on the same page as the target. Screenshots belong to image-based identification, which is a separate method.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A control has no usable properties of its own, but sits directly beside a unique static label on the same screen. What should you try before image-based identification?

options.text: Anchor-based identification, using the label as the anchor control.
Nothing — image-based is the only remaining option.
Enable self-healing and rerun.
Delete and rescan the whole application.

practiceQuiz.hint: A unique neighbour on the same page is exactly what one method is designed to exploit.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Anchor-based identification locates the target relative to a stable neighbouring element, and a unique static label on the same page satisfies all three anchor conditions. It remains a structural method, so it is more robust than falling back on appearance matching.

XScan → select control → Identification methods pane → ADVANCED IDENTIFICATION → IMAGE.
For controls where nothing else works — documented as a last resort.
Use more than one screenshot, especially when the control doesn't always look the same.
Resolution, display scaling, theme, rendering differences, redesigns — none of which structural methods care about.
Identifies by position relative to another element. Anchor must be text or image · unique · same page.
Properties → anchor → alternative engine → custom control → image.
